title: AP Seminar
summary: Evaluate arguments, connect perspectives and build a supported written or spoken case.
frameworkNote: Checked against the official course page on 15 October 2026 for 2026-27. This is an original five-part skill sequence across inquiry, analysis, perspectives, synthesis and communication, not prescribed units. Practice scenarios do not replace required source materials, student-authored assessments or the course’s collaboration and process requirements.

modules.title: Turn a topic into a researchable issue
modules.focus: Ask a question that permits evidence and competing views.
explanation: A useful inquiry question makes its scope clear and allows more than one defensible response. “School meals” is a topic. “How should one school balance cost, access and food waste in its lunch service?” identifies a decision and criteria that can be investigated.

Search terms should include alternative descriptions and opposing positions, not only your preferred answer. Record who created each source, its purpose and the evidence it supplies. Credibility is relevant to a particular claim: expertise in nutrition does not automatically establish expertise in school budgeting.

workedExample.prompt: Improve “Why should all schools ban packaging?”
steps: Remove the assumed answer and define a setting.
Ask “Which packaging changes could reduce waste at this school while preserving food safety and access?”

misconception.claim: A research question is strongest when it already contains the conclusion.
misconception.correction: An open question makes room for evaluation rather than confirmation alone.

questions.prompt: Why search for evidence against a preferred policy?
questions.hint: Consider the quality of the eventual decision.
questions.answer: It reveals trade-offs, implementation barriers and alternative explanations that a one-sided search may miss.
checkpoints: Includes competing evidence
Connects it to evaluation

questions.prompt: What makes expertise claim-specific?
questions.answer: A source’s experience must be relevant to the particular topic and method supporting the claim.
checkpoints: Links expertise to claim
Avoids general authority

questions.prompt: Narrow 'Are cities good?' into a researchable transport question.
questions.answer: Ask how two routes affect travel time in a specified district. Define the relevant users and period. Compare evidence without assuming one route superior.
checkpoints: Ask how two routes affect travel time in a specified district.
Define the relevant users and period.
Compare evidence without assuming one route superior.

questions.prompt: Why would a student's experience alone not settle the route question?
questions.hint: Distinguish an account from a distribution.
hints: Distinguish an account from a distribution.
questions.answer: One experience can identify a barrier. It cannot establish how common that barrier is. Broader journey evidence is needed for population claims.
checkpoints: One experience can identify a barrier.
It cannot establish how common that barrier is.
Broader journey evidence is needed for population claims.

notes.title: Turn a topic into a researchable issue in depth
paragraphs: A researchable issue contains a decision or uncertainty that evidence can address. Narrowing a topic requires specifying a setting, affected people and a meaningful outcome. A question that assumes a policy is beneficial restricts the search before evidence is examined. Different lenses can reveal different consequences, but they should remain connected to the same issue. Record terms used in searching and retain credible disagreement. The purpose of initial inquiry is to discover the shape of the problem, including whether the proposed question needs revision.

steps: Specify a setting and a contested outcome: uniform-cost assistance at one school.
Ask how alternative assistance schemes affect access and administrative cost.
workedExamples.conclusion: The resulting comparison can use documented costs and participant experiences without assuming a preferred scheme.

flashcards.back: It assumes the desired answer.
The setting, population and issue.
They reveal connected but different consequences.
It tests the proposed explanation.

diagrams.title: Scoping uniform assistance
diagrams.description: A broad topic becomes an evidence-based comparison.

nodes.label: Assistance options
nodes.detail: A comparison of benefits and administration.

modules.title: Map a line of reasoning
modules.focus: Separate claims, evidence and the link between them.
explanation: An argument advances a claim using evidence and reasoning. The warrant is the connection explaining why that evidence supports the claim. A statistic can be accurate while the inference drawn from it is weak, so evaluate the logical bridge as well as the source.

A summary reports what an author says; analysis explains how the argument works and where it succeeds or fails. Trace intermediate claims rather than jumping from one quotation to the conclusion. Watch for an untested shift from correlation to cause or from one example to a universal rule.

workedExample.prompt: Analyse “Students who use the library score higher, so requiring library visits will raise everyone’s scores.”
steps: Identify the evidence as an association between use and scores.
Identify the unsupported leap to causation and universal benefit; prior motivation or access could influence both variables.

misconception.claim: More statistics automatically produce stronger reasoning.
misconception.correction: Evidence must be relevant and connected to the conclusion through defensible inference.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between evidence and a warrant?
questions.answer: Evidence supplies information; a warrant explains why that information supports the claim.
checkpoints: Defines both
Explains their relationship

questions.prompt: How could the library claim be narrowed?
questions.answer: In the studied group, library use was associated with higher scores; the data alone do not show that visits caused the difference.
checkpoints: Preserves the finding
Removes causal overreach

questions.prompt: Invented argument: 'The hall is full, so tickets are too cheap.' Identify the missing warrant.
questions.hint: Attendance alone does not measure price.
hints: Attendance alone does not measure price.
questions.answer: The claim assumes full attendance indicates underpricing. A small capacity or popular event could also fill the hall. Price evidence is needed to support the conclusion.
checkpoints: The claim assumes full attendance indicates underpricing.
A small capacity or popular event could also fill the hall.
Price evidence is needed to support the conclusion.

questions.prompt: A report has accurate attendance figures but no learning data. How can you use it responsibly?
questions.answer: Use it to describe attendance. Do not treat attendance as demonstrated learning. Seek learning evidence for a claim about educational effects.
checkpoints: Use it to describe attendance.
Do not treat attendance as demonstrated learning.
Seek learning evidence for a claim about educational effects.

notes.title: Map a line of reasoning in depth
paragraphs: A line of reasoning links claims through evidence and warrants. Map the argument by asking what each statement is doing: offering a conclusion, reporting information, supplying a connecting assumption or acknowledging a limit. A warrant may be unstated and still essential. For example, using survey satisfaction to justify a policy assumes satisfaction is a relevant measure of success. Evaluating reasoning therefore requires checking the evidence's quality and the relevance of that assumption. Accurate data can still support an invalid inference when the connection is weak.

workedExamples.prompt: Invented claim: 'The club has twice as many members, so its teaching must be better.'
steps: Membership growth is the evidence; improved teaching is the conclusion.
The warrant assumes growth reflects teaching quality, overlooking publicity or lower fees.
workedExamples.conclusion: The evidence establishes growth, while the quality claim needs additional measures.

flashcards.back: The link explaining why evidence supports a claim.

flashcards.front: Can true evidence support a weak inference?
flashcards.back: Yes, when the connecting assumption fails.
An intermediate claim supporting a larger conclusion.

flashcards.front: What does an argument map reveal?
flashcards.back: Dependencies and unsupported leaps.

diagrams.title: Membership inference
diagrams.description: The conclusion depends on an untested assumption.

modules.title: Compare perspectives through shared criteria
modules.focus: Explain disagreement rather than listing opinions.
explanation: Perspectives differ because people may have different goals, assumptions, evidence or experiences. A stakeholder label is not itself an argument. Identify what a particular source claims and why, then compare it with another view using a shared issue or criterion.

Avoid false balance: two views do not deserve equal evidential weight merely because both exist. Evaluate the quality and relevance of their support. A strong comparison can recognise a legitimate concern while explaining why another conclusion is better supported for the stated purpose.

workedExample.prompt: Compare two fictional views on later school starts.
steps: One source prioritises reported sleep needs; another highlights transport and after-school scheduling.
Compare benefits, feasibility and affected groups, then seek evidence for each concern rather than treating disagreement as simple selfishness.

misconception.claim: Comparing perspectives means giving every claim equal credibility.
misconception.correction: Fair representation still permits different judgements about evidence quality.

questions.prompt: What is missing from “Parents disagree with students”?
questions.answer: The actual claims, reasons, evidence and diversity within each group are missing.
checkpoints: Requires arguments
Recognises within-group variation

questions.prompt: Name a shared criterion for comparing start-time proposals.
questions.hint: Use a measure applicable to both.
questions.answer: Impact on student access to transport, assessed for each proposal using the same constraints.
checkpoints: Uses a common criterion
Links it to evidence

questions.prompt: Two fictional writers favour an arts grant for different reasons: jobs and cultural access. Explain their relationship.
questions.hint: Compare reasons as well as conclusions.
hints: Compare reasons as well as conclusions.
questions.answer: They agree on funding. One prioritises employment while the other prioritises access. Different priorities may produce disagreement over which projects receive funds.
checkpoints: They agree on funding.
One prioritises employment while the other prioritises access.
Different priorities may produce disagreement over which projects receive funds.

questions.prompt: How would you avoid false balance when one grant claim has audited costs and another has an unsupported estimate?
questions.answer: Describe both estimates. Give greater weight to the transparent audited calculation. Explain the unsupported estimate's uncertainty rather than treating them as equivalent.
checkpoints: Describe both estimates.
Give greater weight to the transparent audited calculation.
Explain the unsupported estimate's uncertainty rather than treating them as equivalent.

notes.title: Compare perspectives through shared criteria in depth
paragraphs: A perspective consists of a position supported by reasons and assumptions, not merely a person's identity. Two members of the same group may disagree, while people in different groups may share a criterion. Compare perspectives using the same question: who benefits, who bears a cost and which evidence supports each prediction? Do not manufacture equal credibility when one claim lacks support. A fair comparison represents the strongest relevant reasoning on each side and then explains why the evidence warrants different weights or a qualified judgement.

workedExamples.prompt: Compare invented proposals for a shared hall: a sports club wants evening practice; a residents' group wants quiet after nine.
steps: Both concern the same space but prioritise access and disturbance respectively.
Compare schedules using participation, noise and feasible closing times.
workedExamples.conclusion: A shared timetable can be evaluated against both concerns instead of treating the groups as mutually hostile.

flashcards.back: No; identify the actual position and reasons.
Shared criteria and accurate representation.

flashcards.front: Must all claims receive equal weight?
flashcards.back: No; evidential quality matters.
Groups do not hold a single uniform view.

nodes.label: Practice access
nodes.detail: The club needs usable evening time.

modules.title: Synthesize a qualified argument
modules.focus: Make sources interact to support your own reasoning.
explanation: Synthesis combines sources around an analytical claim rather than presenting one summary after another. One source may establish a problem, another test a solution and a third reveal a limitation. Explain those relationships in your own reasoning while retaining clear attribution.

A counterargument should address a serious challenge, not a deliberately weak version of the opposing view. You may qualify the proposal, limit its scope or explain why the challenge does not outweigh the evidence. The conclusion should follow from the argument you actually developed.

workedExample.prompt: Build a recommendation from a waste audit and an access interview.
steps: Use the audit to identify a particular waste source.
Use the interview to check whether the proposed remedy excludes some learners, then revise the recommendation to include an accessible alternative.

misconception.claim: Synthesis means placing several citations at the end of a paragraph.
misconception.correction: The paragraph must explain how the sources relate and what conclusion follows.

questions.prompt: How can a source limit another source’s conclusion?
questions.hint: Consider differences in population or conditions.
questions.answer: It may show that a benefit found in one setting depends on resources absent in another.
checkpoints: Identifies a condition
Explains the relationship

questions.prompt: What distinguishes qualification from contradiction?
questions.answer: Qualification limits when or where a claim applies without necessarily rejecting it altogether.
checkpoints: Explains scope
Keeps the logical distinction

questions.prompt: One fictional study finds online access useful; another studies households without reliable internet. Synthesize them.
questions.answer: Online access can help connected households. Connectivity limits transfer to the second group. A recommendation should include equivalent access for households lacking reliable internet.
checkpoints: Online access can help connected households.
Connectivity limits transfer to the second group.
A recommendation should include equivalent access for households lacking reliable internet.

questions.prompt: Why is quoting three sources consecutively not sufficient synthesis?
hints: Ask what conclusion follows from their interaction.
questions.answer: Consecutive quotations may remain separate summaries. Synthesis explains agreement, tension or limitation. That relationship must support the writer's own conclusion.
checkpoints: Consecutive quotations may remain separate summaries.
Synthesis explains agreement, tension or limitation.
That relationship must support the writer's own conclusion.

notes.title: Synthesize a qualified argument in depth
paragraphs: Synthesis involves a new argument built through relationships among sources. A source may provide a general pattern, another may reveal an exception, and a third may explain why the exception occurs. Keep their settings and methods visible so that apparent agreement is not manufactured by ignoring differences. Your conclusion should state how the combined evidence changes the answer to the question. Qualification is substantive when it identifies a condition that matters; adding 'sometimes' without explaining when or why does little analytical work.

workedExamples.prompt: Invented findings: weekend classes attract workers, but interviews identify childcare as a barrier.
steps: The attendance pattern supports weekend availability for some workers.
The interviews limit the inference that timing alone ensures access.
workedExamples.conclusion: Recommend testing childcare support alongside weekend provision, with uptake assessed separately.

flashcards.back: Reasoned interaction among sources.
It reveals conditions limiting a general claim.
Hedging without specifying a meaningful condition.
The writer integrating the sources.

diagrams.title: Access beyond scheduling
diagrams.description: One finding limits the scope of another.

nodes.label: Childcare barrier
nodes.detail: Timing does not remove every constraint.

nodes.label: Combined proposal
nodes.detail: Test support for both scheduling and care.

modules.title: Communicate and collaborate accountably
modules.focus: Make the evidence understandable and contributions traceable.
explanation: A presentation should organise the audience’s attention around the question, reasoning and conclusion. Use a chart only when it clarifies a relationship, and label its source and units. Reading a dense slide aloud usually obscures the argument rather than explaining it.

In group work, agree on roles and deadlines while sharing the reasoning across sections. Keep a record of contributions and revisions so each person can explain how the final argument developed. In an oral response, answer the question directly, use evidence and acknowledge a limit when it matters.

workedExample.prompt: A group presentation has four disconnected source summaries. Revise its structure.
steps: Choose one shared question and organise sections around the main claims.
Add explicit transitions explaining how each section supports or qualifies the group’s conclusion, then rehearse questions across roles.

misconception.correction: Collaboration also requires shared decisions, integration and reflection on the argument.

questions.prompt: What should a chart caption include?
questions.answer: The measure, units, population or timeframe where relevant, and a traceable source.
checkpoints: Includes context
Includes attribution

questions.prompt: How should a speaker handle a question outside the evidence?
questions.answer: State the relevant finding, explain the limit and identify what additional evidence would be needed.
checkpoints: Answers honestly
Names a next evidential step

questions.prompt: A teammate changes the final recommendation after rehearsal. What should the group do?
questions.answer: Review whether evidence supports the new recommendation. Update connected slides and explanations. Record the change and agree responsibilities.
checkpoints: Review whether evidence supports the new recommendation.
Update connected slides and explanations.
Record the change and agree responsibilities.

questions.prompt: An audience asks whether your trial will work nationally. Answer within a single-school design.
questions.answer: The trial provides evidence in one school. National effectiveness remains untested. Replication in varied settings would help assess transfer.
checkpoints: The trial provides evidence in one school.
National effectiveness remains untested.
Replication in varied settings would help assess transfer.

notes.title: Communicate and collaborate accountably in depth
paragraphs: Communication should preserve the reasoning while making its structure easy to follow. A visual needs a clear claim, readable labels and enough context to interpret its evidence. Group collaboration requires more than dividing slides: members need to understand the shared argument and how their contributions connect. Record decisions and changes so that contributions remain traceable. During questions, distinguish an answer supported by evidence from a plausible extension. Acknowledging a limit and explaining the next evidence needed is more credible than inventing certainty under pressure.

workedExamples.prompt: An invented presentation shows a bar marked '80' and says participation improved. Repair the slide.
steps: Label the measure as participants and show the comparison period or baseline.
Add the source and explain whether the increase represents new people or repeat visits.
workedExamples.conclusion: The slide can support a participation claim only when its unit and comparison are visible.

flashcards.back: Measure, units, comparison context and source.

flashcards.front: What should a group decision log preserve?
flashcards.back: Choices, reasons and contributions.
State the limit and needed evidence.
Members must understand the shared argument.

diagrams.title: A defensible presentation claim
diagrams.description: Context turns a number into interpretable evidence.

nodes.label: Supported comparison
nodes.detail: A clear change against a comparable baseline.
